title: Art Tatum, soloists and small-group playing
summary: They discuss Tatum, spontaneity, and whether she'd sing with a pianist like him, recalling a Boston bill with him.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: I think another name is Art Tatum, he was one of the giant soloists, as far as I know, never played with a band.
So he was never contrained by that - the discipline involved.

Oh, well, there are a few recordings that Art made with the rhythm section and they couldn't keep up with Art because he was so spontaneous. I mean there was no way that you could keep up with what was going on in his head. And of course that stuff was never written down. The guys get in there, they just have to follow or else and if you listen closely there were a lot of times when they couldn't keep up with Art and his changes, you know, they just had to lay out.

Well, that's been said about him but I think some people would say that he was also a good small group player when he accompanied -- well later on in his career he played with Ben Webster, with Roy Eldridge He accompanied Joe Turner, the blues singer --

I believe that -- you know there's a certain area where musicians and performers are simpatico, they can almost anticipate what the other person is going to play -- if you understand their basic, their progressions, they know how far they can improvise and how far they can

extend the particular chord without getting into too much dissonance so it's very understandable that I could and did work with these guys and accompanied them -- and it's very difficult to say who was influenced by whom. See, the instrumentalists were listening to Art and being led into these changes by Art. Certainly Art was not following them. That I could feel for certain. We knew we were following Art and glad to be able to, you know.
Could you conceive of yourself singing on the records with Art Tatum behind you as for instance you did record with Ellis Larkins (phonetic spelling).
That was the same instrumentation as the trio that Art Tatum led in the early to mid '40s.

Right. I worked on a bill with Art Tatum in Boston when George Wein had Storyville and we had a few sessions together. He was crazy about 'If I Had a Ribbon Bow,' and of course if, say for instance I was going to make a recording with Art Tatum we would certainly -- it

wouldn't be that spontaneous. You know, we wouldn't just sit out there "come on, let's go," knowing that Art would -- I'm pretty sure that Art would listen to me but I would prefer to be guided by Art, but I'd have to know, okay, what are we going to do when we get to this bar so I'll know what to do. But then, so far as I'm concerned if you'll listen to that recording that I made with the New Friends of Rhythm that's a lot of way-out stuff. All I had to do was stick to the melody so it really doesn't matter if I'm not going to improvise what's behind me. I mean, my job is to stick to the melody.
